prospect.name: Eddy
prospect.location: Northern Michigan, USA — lives on 60 acres; Eastern time zone
prospect.occupation: Founder of a company he is currently starting and has just begun taking a salary from; also serves in the Marine Corps Reserve. Describes himself as a salesperson — 'I close every day. I'm a sales guy pretty much.'
prospect.family_status: Married; son turning 1 next month (born on Eddy's own birthday, 39 years apart) and daughter aged 3. Wife and mother-in-law do most of the cooking.
prospect.training_background: Former college athlete, long-serving Marine Corps reservist who trains for USMC fitness tests. Trains almost daily at home and has not used a gym since COVID. Pull-ups, EMOMs, burpees, dumbbells, kettlebell swings, 400s and 800s, occasional three-mile runs, rucking, mountain biking and indoor cycling for Zone 2. Competitive canoe racing is his next endurance target, with a major race planned in about a year. Comfortable with swings but not with snatches or clean and press. Has been coached before, in both fitness and business, and says he performs best under supervision.
prospect.medical: Torn both ACLs (bilateral). Running is painful and he now avoids it in favour of low-impact endurance work — 'I just don't think it's worth the pounding that my knees and ankles and hips take.' Explicitly worried about needing knee replacements in his fifties. Weight has crept from ~180 to 190 lb over recent years. No other conditions disclosed. NOTE: the rep never asked an injury or health-condition question directly; the ACL history surfaced only because he asked 'Why is it painful?' about running, and it was never followed up — whether the ACLs were surgically reconstructed, and whether loaded ballistic work is appropriate, were never established.

signals: Already fit and self-aware about it — 'I'm not really that far off, I'm not in that bad of shape, I just want to get better, you know?'
Explicitly good-to-great: 'I could reach my goals in like three months if I was dialed in for sure'
Successful and building — starting a company, owns 60 acres, recently bought a $10,000 tractor and another $10,000 item
Treats price as a quality signal rather than an insult: 'I think that's a fair price... that's probably the price I'd be charging if I were him as well'

Buying supervision rather than information — 'I perform the best when I'm being coached and I'm being supervised... I've been at my best in my life when I've had people just tell me what I need to do'

QUALIFIER on confidence: price did function as a barrier on this call, which cuts against the archetype's 'price is not a barrier'. The constraint is cashflow timing from a company he has only just started drawing a salary from, plus a psychological threshold about the size of the single outgoing, rather than any doubt about worth.

goals.text: Still be moving really well and functionally fit as a grandfather in his seventies
Drop 15-20 pounds from his current 190 and get back to where he was
Be the person he should be for his one-year-old son and three-year-old daughter, with 30+ years of parenting ahead
Keep doing endurance sports for a long time — canoe racing, rucking, mountain biking, skiing
Be pushed the extra 20% he cannot push himself — 'I need somebody helping push me and program for me and call me on my [expletive]'
Get technically competent at kettlebell snatches, cleans and presses, which he is not comfortable with
Be stronger, more jacked, better cardio, lower body fat
Avoid needing knee replacements in his fifties
Teach his kids to ski, ruck and hike with them, and be outdoors with them daily
Stop the five-pounds-a-year creep before it becomes 200, 210, 220

pains.text: Self-negotiates down in every solo session — 'it's easy to cut the sets a little short. Nobody's telling me what to do. Nobody's going to know.'
Five years of training alone producing what he calls mediocre results relative to effort
No programming — picks workouts on the spot and they end up not being hard enough
Weight creeping up roughly five pounds a year since marriage and kids
Nutrition consistency: eats his kids' food, eats whatever is cooked for him, and will 'smash eight pieces' of pizza when it appears
Bilateral torn ACLs making running painful and raising fear of joint replacement in his fifties
Not confident with kettlebell snatches, cleans and presses despite training with kettlebells regularly
Self-doubt about his own follow-through — 'I've been working on doing this my whole life, and I've mostly at least got okay results, but never fully succeeded'
Cashflow squeeze from starting a company and only just beginning to take a salary
Falls off diet away from home — at the in-laws, eating out

objections.raw_quote: I think the coaching I've had in the past, which is, I agree, probably not at that standard, was like $500 a month, and I think that's the price I have in my head, and it's $6,000 up front. Is that accurate? Or is it $1,000 a month?
objections.rep_response: Did not address the $500/month anchor at all. Answered only the payment-structure half of the question — 'Most of the guys put it up front just for themselves... but if there's like some financial obstacles for you right now that you cannot put it up front, we can talk about how to structure that.' The anchor resurfaced eleven minutes later still unaddressed: 'probably because all the coaching I've had is usually like 500 a month.'

objections.raw_quote: Let me talk to my wife, and I just got I'll make sure
objections.rep_response: Opened by dismissing it outright — 'So don't give me the, the, the wife objections' — then recovered and ran the strongest scripted move: 'is it really that you're asking her for permission, or, you know, you're just figuring out the financials?' and 'when you talk to her, what do you think, what she's going to say about it?' The prospect conceded it was 'mostly figuring out the financials'. The deposit-with-full-refund fallback was never offered.

objections.raw_quote: Let me think about it. I got to think about it at six grand. I agree. It makes sense. And I understand. I would want, I would, that's probably the price I'd be charging if I were him as well. It's just not the amount that I was, that I committed to.
objections.rep_response: Worked persistently across roughly fifteen minutes. Ran the belief question ('do you feel like what we've gone through today can actually get you to your goals?'), pressed the hedge ('Probably?' / 'what could happen that it wouldn't work?'), isolated the blocker ('what's stopping you? Is it that the budget is tight or what is it?'), and applied pressure variants not in the script ('You want me to give up on you that easily?', 'You cannot or you don't want to commit?'). Did not run the decisive scripted moves — 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is' and 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now?'.

objections.raw_quote: yeah, the budget is tight. So I'm starting a company and I'm just starting to take a salary and that's a huge part of it. just making sure that this is the right thing to do pretty much.
objections.rep_response: Reframed the question from financial to volitional — 'But is it the right thing to do in terms of finances or actually doing it? Because from what I understand, you want to do this.' Did not run any of the OD timing moves and did not return to the split-payment structure he had offered earlier, which was the obvious answer to a startup cashflow constraint.

objections.raw_quote: I guess it's on my own, probably, like, self-deprecating understanding of my own capabilities, being like, I guess there's a chance it wouldn't work. ... there's always a level of self-doubt that it's going to creep into anything.
objections.rep_response: Ran OE properly. Named it — 'Would it be fair to say that you're looking for certainty that if you do what Trevor teaches would actually get you there?' — and closed it with 'how can actually you be certain if you don't try, especially with fitness, right? Because it's your body.' The prospect agreed: 'that's some logic there.' The rep also introduced a guarantee at this point, which the prospect welcomed ('I like the guarantee. I think that helps') without it changing his decision.

objections.raw_quote: I don't think I have any questions about the value that Trevor would provide and the programs would provide. I just have to get used to the fact of having $6,000 go out of my bank accounts pretty much. That's probably the biggest aspect.
objections.rep_response: The best-handled objection of the call. The rep isolated it correctly ('Is it the money thing or something else that you're still not sure about the value that you're getting?'), confirmed the money existed, and then ran a regret frame that visibly moved the prospect: 'In 5, 10 years, 15 years, are you going to still remember this 6K that you spent? When you're going to be freaking healthy and showing up for your family every single day?' Prospect: 'That's a good point... I like that pitch. I mean, the answer would be no, I wouldn't.' It still did not close him.

offer.payment_plan_terms: Splitting was offered twice in principle but never structured or quantified — 'if there's like some financial obstacles for you right now that you cannot put it up front, we can talk about how to structure that' and 'So what's your take? You want to split it?'. The prospect did not take it up and the rep did not return to it, so no terms, deposit, instalment count or schedule were ever discussed. Continuation beyond six months was confirmed as available but unpriced.
offer.guarantee_mentioned: Introduced live and mid-objection, prefaced by the rep appearing to recall it in the moment: 'well, I have I that, when I think about it, there's also a guarantee. And not a lot of guys, I think, actually in this space can give you a guarantee on that, that you will reach your goals within six months, and there's like a science behind that, that you will add at least eight kilos, which is around 17 pounds, to your baseline kettlebell weight movements. And that's combined with the proper nutrition that you're going to follow and showing up for the workouts, you're going to reach your goals. If that wouldn't happen, Trevor is going to work with you until you do for free.' When the prospect sought confirmation ('So you're saying that I would reach my goals or Trevor continues to work with me past six months for free?'), the rep extended the scope beyond the strength metric to the weight-loss goal: 'Yeah, if you wouldn't reach your goal. And you wouldn't lose the 15, 20 pounds in that six months.' Two materially different guarantees were therefore stated within about thirty seconds.

evidence: No payment taken, no payment link sent, no agreement raised

Repeated, explicit and unambiguous refusal to decide on the call — 'I don't think I'd commit to $6,000 right now', 'I don't think you can get me over the line on this call', 'I still need a little time'
Strong positive intent and no value objection — 'I don't think I have any questions about the value that Trevor would provide', 'I do believe in you guys', 'I would like to do this'
Voluntarily committed to not disappearing: 'I won't completely ghost you. I'll follow up for sure'
Concrete next step agreed and tested live — the rep sent a WhatsApp message during the call and had the prospect confirm receipt ('Got it'), and a 16:00 Eastern callback the same day was agreed
COUNTER-EVIDENCE: he is actively shopping at least two other coaches, one an ex-coach he used six years ago and one a CrossFit coach who has not yet replied

COUNTER-EVIDENCE: he is a professional salesperson, was openly narrating the tactics as they were used ('I know all your strategies, bro'), and gave several warm-sounding statements that were explicitly not commitments
COUNTER-EVIDENCE: the rep leaves on vacation the following day, so the same-evening WhatsApp is effectively the only live window before August
outcome.next_step: Rep to message Eddy on WhatsApp at approximately 16:00 Eastern the same day. Eddy to speak to his wife and 'see if I can put together something that I can get to'. If not resolved that evening, the conversation resumes in August after the rep's vacation.

notable.note: Two things a principal should see. First, a guarantee was produced live and mid-objection, apparently from memory, and then restated with a materially wider scope thirty seconds later — from '+8 kg on baseline kettlebell movements' to 'you wouldn't lose the 15, 20 pounds', with free continued coaching until achieved as the remedy. Whether that guarantee exists in this form, and which version is contractual, needs an immediate ruling. Second, this is the closest fit to the stated ICP anywhere in the batch — company founder, former college athlete, Marine reservist, explicitly good-to-great, spends $10,000 on farm equipment without ceremony — and he did not buy, while prospects well outside the ICP have closed at full price. Also worth noting: the rep told the prospect 'I'm also 40' during the nutrition section, then said 'I'm 43 right now' fifteen minutes later. The best moment of the call was the future-regret frame; the worst was opening the spouse objection with 'don't give me the wife objections'.

quality.notes: Extensive swapping. The most consequential inversions sit at the close of the pillar presentation and the start of the objection sequence: 'So if we can figure out all the technical logistical details, are you fully committed to showing up and doing the work?' at 00:27:57 is the rep but is labelled Eddy, and 'All right, so let's make this deal happen' is the reverse. The entire price reveal at 00:28:35 — 'as I mentioned, the full transformation takes six months... the investment is $6K' — is labelled Eddy but is unmistakably the rep. Several short exchanges around 00:31:31 to 00:33:09 alternate incorrectly. Roles were assigned from content throughout. Prospect's surname is never spoken.
